items.title: Step 1
items.description:
In this workshop, you'll implement a linked list.

To begin, create a function named `initList`. Inside it, return an object with a `head` property set to `null`, and a `length` property of `0`.

This is the function you will call to initialize a linked list. The `head` represents the first element in the list, initially, it is `null` because there's no element in the list. The `length` tracks the number of nodes (elements) in the list, which you will increment or decrement when adding or removing a node from the list.

hints.text: You should create an `initList` function.
hints.test: assert.isFunction(initList)

hints.text: Your `initList` function should return an object.
hints.test: assert.isObject(initList());

hints.text: Your `initList` function should return an object with a `head` set to `null`.
hints.test: assert.propertyVal(initList(), "head", null);

hints.text: Your `initList` function should return an object with a `length` set to `0`.
hints.test: assert.propertyVal(initList(), "length", 0);

items.title: Step 2
items.description:
The next thing you will work on is a function that lets you check if the list is empty.

To do that, create a function named `isEmpty` that takes a `list` parameter. Inside the function, return a check to see if the `length` property of `list` is strictly equal to `0`.

hints.text: You should create an `isEmpty` function.
hints.test: assert.isFunction(isEmpty)

hints.text: Your `isEmpty` function should have a `list` parameter.
Your `isEmpty` function should return `list.length === 0`.

items.title: Step 3
items.description:
Now you will work on the function that will add a node to the list.

Create an `add` function with `list` and `element` parameters.

hints.text: You should create an `add` function.
hints.test: assert.isFunction(add)

hints.text: Your `add` function should have `list` and `element` parameters.

items.title: Step 4
items.description:
This node would need two properties, the element to add, and a pointer to the next node.

Inside the add function, create an object named `node`, it should have a property named `element`, and a `next` property set to `null`, which is the pointer to the next element of the list.

hints.text: You should create an object named `node` inside your `add` function.
Your `node` object should have a property named `element` set to `element`.
Your `node` object should have a property named `next` set to `null`.

items.title: Step 5
items.description:
At this point, you should test the linked list for better understanding.

Create a `myList` variable and set it to `initList()`. Under it, log a call of `isEmpty()` using `myList` as the parameter to the console. Then, after that, call `add` with `myList` and a number of your choice, then log `myList` to the console. Under that, log another call of `isEmpty()` to the console using `myList` as the parameter again.

hints.text: You should create a `myList` variable set to `initList()`.
hints.test: assert.deepEqual(myList, initList());

hints.text: You should log a call to `isEmpty(myList)` to the console.
You should call `add` with `myList` and a number of your choice as the parameters.
You should log your `myList` variable to the console.
You should log `isEmpty(myList)` to the console again.

items.title: Step 6
items.description:
Notice the `true`, `{ head: null, length: 0 }`, and `true` results in the console? This happens because you've not assigned anything to the list `myList`, and you've not incremented the `length` property.

Go ahead and assign `node` to `list.head`, and under that, increment the `length` property of `list`.

hints.text: You should assign `node` to `list.head`.
You should increment the `length` property of `list`.

items.title: Step 7
items.description:
Now, the log should show something like `{ head: { element: 42, next: null }, length: 1 }` in the console. 

However, this is not how you would handle a case where the added node is the first element in the list, that is, the head.

To do that properly, use an if statement to check if the list is empty by calling the `isEmpty` function with the `list`. If that's true, then move your `list.head = node` line into the body of the `if` statement.

hints.text: You should have an `if` statement with the condition `isEmpty(list)`.
You should move your `list.head = node` line into the `if` statement.

items.title: Step 8
items.description:
If the list is not empty, then you want to find its end, add the new element there, and make it point to `null`. This means you have to loop through the list from the `head`.

To start that, open up an `else` clause. Inside it, use `let` to create a `current` variable and set it to `list.head`.

hints.text: You should have an `else` clause.
You should create a `current` variable set to `list.head` inside the `else` clause.

items.title: Step 9
items.description: Now, create a `while` loop with `current.next !== null` as the condition. This means the loop should keep running as long as the current node has another node after it.

hints.text: You should create a `while` loop with the condition `current.next !== null`.

items.title: Step 10
items.description: Inside the `while` loop, update `current` to `current.next` so the loop moves forward through the list one node at a time, and stops when it reaches the node with a `next` property of `null`, that is, the end of the list.

hints.text: You should update the value of your `current` variable to `current.next` inside the `while` loop.

items.title: Step 11
items.description: After finding the last node, you need to attach the new node to it. To do that, set `current.next` to `node` under the while loop but still within the `else` clause.

hints.text: You should set `current.next` to `node` under your `while` loop.

items.title: Step 12
items.description: That's all you need to add an element to the list. To see what things look like, add two more numbers of your choice to the `myList` list.

hints.text: You should add two more numbers of your choice to the `myList` list.

items.title: Step 13
items.description:
Now, you will work on a function to remove a node from the list.

Create a `remove` function with `list` and `element` parameters.

hints.text: You should create a `remove` function.
hints.test: assert.isFunction(remove)

hints.text: Your `remove` function should have `list` and `element` parameters.

items.title: Step 14
items.description:
Inside the `remove` function, use `let` to create a `previous` variable set to `null`, and `let` again to create a `current` variable set to `list.head`. These are the variables you will use in the loop that will traverse the list.

`current` tracks the node currently being checked in the list, starting at the head and moving forward one node at a time. `previous`, on the other hand, keeps track of the node right before the current one.

This is important when removing a node because you must update the next value of the previous node so it points to the node after the one being removed, in order to keep the list connected.

hints.text: You should use `let` to create a `previous` variable set to `null` inside your `remove` function.
You should use `let` to create a `current` variable set to `list.head` inside your `remove` function.

items.title: Step 15
items.description:
Now, create a `while` loop that checks if `current` is not strictly `null` and `current.element` is not strictly equal to element.

This means the loop should continue traversing the list until the end of the list is reached or the element to remove is found.

hints.text: You should create a `while` loop with the condition `current !== null && current.element !== element`.

items.title: Step 16
items.description: Inside the loop, reassign `previous` to `current`, and `current` to `current.next`. This means `current` checks the next node, and `previous` always stays one node behind.

hints.text: You should reassign the `previous` variable to `current`.
You should reassign the `current` variable to `current.next`.

items.title: Step 17
items.description:
If `current` is `null`, it means that's the end of the list, so the function should stop running.

Create an `if` statement that checks if `current` is strictly equal to `null`. Inside the `if` statement, use `return` to exit the function.

hints.text: You should create an `if` statement with the condition `current === null`.
You should use the `return` keyword inside your `if` statement.

items.title: Step 18
items.description:
If `previous` is not `null`, this means the element to be removed is not at the head but somewhere within the list, so the current node should be bypassed by linking the previous node directly to the next node.

To do that, create another `if` statement that checks if `previous` is strictly not `null`. If that's the case, set `previous.next` to `current.next`.

hints.text: You should create another `if` statement with the condition `previous !== null`.
You should set `previous.next` to `current.next`.

items.title: Step 19
items.description:
If `previous` is `null`, this means the element to be removed is at the head of the list, so you should update the `head` to point to the next node in order to remove the first element.

To do that, add an `else` clause. Inside it, set `list.head` to `current.next`.

hints.text: You should add an `else` clause to your `if` statement.
You should set `list.head` to `current.next` inside the `else` clause.

items.title: Step 20
items.description: Now, you need to decrement `length` in the `remove` function to keep track of the actual number of elements remaining in the list after removing one.

hints.text: You should decrement the `length` property of `list` using the decrement operator (`--`).

items.title: Step 21
items.description:
Now, you should test out the `remove` function.

Remove any of the numbers from the list by calling the `remove` function with `myList` and the number to remove, then log `myList` to the console using `console.log(JSON.stringify(myList, null, 2))` to see the complete updated list.

With that, your linked list workshop is complete!

hints.text: You should remove any of the existing numbers using the `remove` function.
You should log `myList` to the console again, this time using `JSON.stringify(myList, null, 2)`.
